# ansi-regex [![Build Status](https://travis-ci.org/chalk/ansi-regex.svg?branch=master)](https://travis-ci.org/chalk/ansi-regex)

> Regular expression for matching [ANSI escape codes](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code)


## Install

```
$ npm install --save ansi-regex
```


## Usage

```js
const ansiRegex = require('ansi-regex');

ansiRegex().test('\u001b[4mcake\u001b[0m');
//=> true

ansiRegex().test('cake');
//=> false

'\u001b[4mcake\u001b[0m'.match(ansiRegex());
//=> ['\u001b[4m', '\u001b[0m']
```

## FAQ

### Why do you test for codes not in theCMA 48 standard?

Some of the codes we run as a test are codes that we acquired finding various lists of non-standard or manufacturer specificodes. If I recall correctly, we test for both standard and non-standard codes, as most of them follow the same or similar format and can be safely matched in strings withouthe risk of removing actual string content. There are a few non-standard control codes that do not follow the traditional format (i.e. they end inumbers) thus forcing us to exclude them from the test because we cannot reliably match them.

On the historical side, thoseCMA standards werestablished in thearly 90's whereas the VT100, for example, was designed in the mid/late 70's. Athat point in time, control codes were still pretty ungoverned and engineers used them for a multitude of things, namely to activate hardware ports that may have been proprietary. Somewherelse you see a similar 'anarchy' of codes is in the x86 architecture for processors; there are a ton of "interrupts" that can mean differenthings on certain brands of processors, most of whichave been phased out.
